name: The Neoplatonic Trinity: the One, Spirit (nous), and Soul
plain_explanation: Plotinus describes reality as flowing down from a single, indescribable ultimate source (the One), through a divine Mind or Spirit (nous) that contemplates the One and contains the eternal Forms/ideas, down to Soul, which creates and animates the visible physical universe.
precise_definition: Plotinus's metaphysical hierarchy of three unequal hypostases: the One (transcending Being itself, indefinable, sometimes called God or the Good), nous or Spirit (the 'image' of the One, engendered by the One's self-directed vision, containing the world of Forms/ideas), and Soul (the offspring of nous, which creates the visible sensory world, Nature, as its 'downward' image).
why_it_mattered: This structure is, in Russell's account (following Dean Inge), inseparable from Christian theology: 'it is impossible to disagree' that Platonism, largely as mediated by Plotinus, is 'part of the vital structure of Christian theology.'
historical_origin: Systematized by Plotinus (writing from age 49 onward) as a development of Plato's theory of Forms and of the mystical strands in the Phaedo, Republic Book VI, and Symposium.
examples: Origen's contemporaneous, structurally similar (though later heretical) doctrine of the divine Persons' hierarchy
Saint Augustine's admiration for Plato's system as 'the most pure and bright in all philosophy'
competing_positions: The equal-Persons structure of the orthodox Christian Trinity, as distinguished explicitly by Russell from Plotinus's unequal, hierarchical three hypostases
influence_on_later_thinkers: Dean Inge (quoted at length by Russell) argues it is impossible to excise Platonism from Christianity 'without tearing Christianity to pieces'; Saint Thomas Aquinas is said to be, in some respects, 'nearer to Plotinus than to the real Aristotle.'
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Directly and extensively shapes medieval Catholic theology, according to Russell/Dean Inge.
